newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Bethlehem mayor blasts Israel over closure.
newsitem.headline: Bethlehem mayor blasts Israel over closure.

text.p: The Palestinian mayor of Bethlehem said on Monday that Israeli closures on the West Bank and Gaza Strip had cast a shadow on the Christmas spirit in the town of Jesus's birth.
Mayor Elias Freij accused Israel of deliberately trying to destroy the Palestinian economy.
"Last year things were better. Our morale was better, the economic conditions were better and there was no closure," Freij told Reuters in an interview.
"Israel deliberately intends to destroy the Palestinian economy and to weaken the Palestinian cities and drive them to poverty," he said.
Israel handed over six West Bank cities, including Bethlehem, to the PLO last year under a self-rule deal that calls for a gradual end to nearly three decades of Israeli occupation.
Bethlehem celebrated its most joyous Christmas last year when Israel pulled out its troops just days before the holiday.
But Israel imposed a closure, barring Palestinians from jobs in the Jewish state, during a spate of Islamic militant suicide bombings in February and March that killed 59 people in Israel.

Israel says the closure guards the security of its citizens. Palestinians regard it as collective punishment. The closure has since been eased to allow some of the workers to return to work in the Jewish state.

"Before the mayor speaks against the closure, he has to think who caused the closure," said Shlomo Dror, a spokesman for the coordinator of Israeli government activity in the West Bank and Gaza Strip.

"We know that these security measures affect the income and quality of life for people. But if you put people's life on one side and the quality of life on the other, of course we will choose the life of people," he said.
Freij bitterly accused Israel of using security as an excuse to keep Palestinian cities from developing economically.
Palestinians in Bethlehem also complain that tourism, the mainstay for most of the city's 40,000 residents, suffers from Israeli travel restrictions which scare away visitors.
Businessmen say Palestinians from the northern part of the West Bank must travel a long detour road to get to Bethlehem while Gazans are barred altogether.
Freij has complained Bethlehem's strained budget was forcing the city to depend on private donations to decorate the city for Christmas.

Workmen were preparing a foundation opposite Manger Square to put up a 14-metre (42-foot) Christmas tree donated by Finland to the city. City officials said the tree has arrived at an Israeli port and was expected in Bethlehem in a few days.
